n: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Clinical Implications

faq.a: One functional copy can still produce enough protein to control growth; loss of both removes the brake.
faq.q: Why do tumour suppressor genes need both alleles lost?

faq.a: Yes, carriers of germline mutations are at higher risk but may never develop disease without additional hits.
faq.q: Can a patient have a tumour suppressor mutation without cancer?

faq.a: Rely on clinical pattern, tumour type, and family history to infer likely suppressor involvement.
faq.q: What is the first step if molecular testing is unavailable?

exam: A 22‑year‑old with a family history of early‑onset breast cancer presents with a breast mass – what genetic test is indicated and why? — TP53 testing for Li‑Fraumeni; guides surveillance and family counseling.
A child with bilateral retinoblastoma – what tumour suppressor is implicated and what is the long‑term management? — RB1 loss; requires lifelong eye exams and screening for secondary cancers.

In a resource‑limited setting, a patient has a colorectal tumour and numerous polyps – how do you confirm the diagnosis without sequencing? — Clinical count of >100 polyps suggests familial adenomatous polyposis; offer prophylactic colectomy.

A patient with a p53‑mutant lung tumour is not responding to standard chemotherapy – what alternative regimen is preferred? — Platinum‑based agents, as they are less dependent on p53‑mediated apoptosis.

During surgery you encounter a tumour that on frozen section shows loss of RB protein – what does this imply for prognosis? — RB loss often indicates aggressive behaviour, prompting wider resection margins.
A pregnant woman with a known APC mutation develops a large colonic polyp – what is the safest management? — Endoscopic polypectomy if feasible; avoid radiation; plan surgery postpartum if needed.
How does chronic hepatitis B infection relate to tumour suppressor pathways? — HBV integration can inactivate p53, increasing risk of hepatocellular carcinoma; monitor AFP and ultrasound.

A patient on herbal medicine presents with a sarcoma; what should you consider regarding tumour suppressors? — Some herbs contain mutagens that can cause DNA damage and loss of p53 function; advise cessation and assess for exposure.
ai.title: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Clinical Implications
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Tumor suppressor genes normally restrain cell growth; loss leads to cancer. Clinicians must recognize patterns, use appropriate investigations, and manage patients in low‑resource settings.

b: Two‑hit hypothesis – both copies must be lost
Somatic loss often via deletion, mutation, or epigenetic silencing
sections.p: Tumor suppressor genes encode proteins that halt cell division, repair DNA, or trigger apoptosis. When both alleles are inactivated, uncontrolled proliferation can occur, forming malignancies.

b: p53 loss – many solid tumours, aggressive disease
RB1 loss – retinoblastoma, small‑cell lung cancer
APC loss – familial adenomatous polyposis, colorectal cancer
sections.p: Identify cancers where loss of specific suppressors is common and understand how this influences presentation and prognosis.

b: Consider surgery early for high‑risk lesions
Avoid DNA‑damaging chemotherapy if p53‑deficient tumours are known to be resistant
sections.p: Recognising a tumour suppressor defect guides screening, family counselling and therapeutic choices, especially where targeted agents are limited.
In low‑resource hospitals, rely on morphology and clinical pattern when molecular tests are unavailable.

t.b: Does the tumour express the protein? Loss suggests a suppressor defect; guides prognosis

t.a: PCR or sequencing of tumour tissue
t.b: Detects specific mutations (e.g., TP53). Confirms diagnosis when IHC unavailable
Identifies germline carriers; informs screening of relatives
Assesses organ function before surgery or chemotherapy; may reveal paraneoplastic syndromes

b: Platinum‑based chemotherapy for p53‑mutant tumours (more effective than alkylating agents)
Avoid high‑dose cyclophosphamide in p53‑deficient sarcomas due to resistance
sections.p: Treat the tumour first; supportive care follows. Choose drugs that do not rely on intact p53 pathways when possible.

b: Hereditary cancer syndromes from DNA‑repair genes (e.g., BRCA) vs. classic suppressor loss
sections.p: Oncogenes – genes that promote growth when activated, opposite of tumour suppressors.

b: Poor fixation can mask protein loss
Low‑grade tumours may retain some suppressor expression despite mutation
sections.p: Immunohistochemistry may be falsely negative due to technical failure; confirm with molecular testing if possible.

b: Li‑Fraumeni – early‑onset sarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumour; test TP53
FAP – hundreds of colonic polyps; APC mutation, prophylactic colectomy
